This see-through camera lets photographers maintain eye contact with their subjects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:33:03 UTC
00:33:03 KST

Lutra, a South Korean startup, has debuted a new brand called Humans of Authenticity (HOA) that’s launching another screen-free digital camera that incorporates a large open viewfinder into its design, as spotted by PetaPixel. The camera is reminiscent of the Godox C100 but the HOA A1 positions its lens and sensor close to the center of its large viewfinder window so that a photographer can maintain eye contact with their subject, or feel more in the moment while framing a shot without staring at a screen.
This see-through camera lets photographers maintain eye contact with their subjects
The HOA A1 incorporates a large viewfinder into its design so you’re not staring at a screen.
The HOA A1 First Edition is expected to launch on December 1st in a very limited run of just 100 units. Preorders haven’t started yet, but the camera will be priced at 360,000 South Korean won, or $289 for US customers. The A1 features a 16-megapixel, 1/2.53-inch Sony sensor paired with a 26mm f/1.75 lens. There is a tiny LCD display on the back but it’s used to display information like battery life and your remaining shots. Everything else about the camera is strictly point and shoot with a shutter button located on its top edge.
The HOA website doesn’t include extensive details about the camera’s capabilities, or even sample shots captured by the A1. According to the site the company is still “fine-tuning the camera’s color and tone in collaboration with photographers.” It does confirm that instead of copying photos to a device or PC using a USB cable or by removing a memory card, the A1 connects to Wi-Fi and wirelessly makes your shots available by tapping your smartphone to the back of the camera.
A wireless connection to the internet isn’t needed to take photos, but you’ll need access to Wi-Fi to view and download your shots. The A1 uses a system called ShootProof that authenticates every image captured with an anonymous certificate recorded to a public blockchain. That feature doesn’t appear optional, but there’s also a signature mode you can turn on or off that lets you sign your name in an accompanying app and then have it overlaid in the corner of every photo.

Apple has a secret list of banned autocomplete phrases including ‘dictator Trump’ and ‘covid is a hoax’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:10:28 UTC
00:10:28 KST

A researcher found over 100,000 words and phrases in “every major language” that are blocked from autocomplete and swipe-type in iOS, Reuters reports. The researcher, Derik Kauffman, says you can still type the words on the blocklist one letter at a time. But they won’t pop up as predictive text suggestions and iOS’s keyboard may automatically alter them when swipe-typing, like changing “left wing conspiracy” to “left wrong conspiracy.”
Apple has a secret list of banned autocomplete phrases including ‘dictator Trump’ and ‘covid is a hoax’
iOS’s keyboard won’t suggest or swipe-type a lengthy list of insults and political phrases.
Kauffman posted the full list online, including the individual lists for different languages.
Most of the words and phrases on the list are offensive, slurs, or related to topics like sex and drugs. But it also contains political phrases like “illegal immigrant,” “dictator Trump,” “sleepy Joe,” “covid was a hoax,” and “left wing conspiracy” as well as some less controversial phrases like “Santa isn’t real” and “iMessage isn’t working.” Kauffman found some discrepancies on the list, too, where one phrase is blocked while its counterpart isn’t, such as blocking “bad girl” but not “bad boy.”
According to Reuters, Kauffman used OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code to help find the list “deep in the bowels” of iOS. On his website, Kauffman says the phrase list was stored as a hash table, which he was able to convert back to text. Another researcher told Reuters they were able to independently obtain the same list. Apple told Reuters that its keyboard is designed to avoid potentially inappropriate or offensive suggestions, but iPhone users can still type in what they want, or override predictive text suggestions. “Apple did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Fox bought Roku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:08:52 UTC
00:08:52 KST

Fox has officially closed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, the companies announced on Friday. With Roku under its umbrella, Fox now controls a major streaming platform that reaches more than 100 million households in the US.
Fox bought Roku
Fox now has control of Roku’s streaming platform, which reaches more than 100 million US households.
First announced in June, the deal will allow Fox to bring Fox Sports, news content, and local stations to Roku. “I would expect that we can grow our viewership in the US with a combination of Roku technology, Roku’s platform, the tremendous content that’s on The Roku Channel, and the content that Fox brings to it as well,” Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch said at the time. Along with Roku, Fox also operates its own Fox One streaming service and the free streamer Tubi.
Though the deal might change what Roku showcases on its platform, it doesn’t look like it will affect the open nature of Roku’s streaming ecosystem. The Department of Justice says Fox has committed to keeping Roku “an open and neutral content partner post-merger.” That includes allowing Roku to carry non-Fox content for at least three years and not discriminating against rival content in search results. It also committed to continuing to allow users to rearrange the apps and tiles on Roku’s home screen.
“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said. “Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner.” Wood now serves on Fox’s board of directors.
Update, November 6th: Added information from the DOJ.

Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:07:47 UTC
00:07:47 KST

Agentic Identity Broker manages delegation chains for on-behalf-of flows in Agentic AI, bridges distinct OAuth2 infrastructures, and provides a secure token vault. Deployed within the call path via gateways like Agentgateway, it offloads auth burdens from both agent and MCP server creators.
For users, it provides a simple way to manage consent, granting agents granular permissions across services such as Google, GitHub, Databricks, and Linear without compromising control.
- Secure Identity Management
Agent registration, principal authentication, and session management
- OAuth2 Delegation & Consent
Manage OAuth2 scopes and user consent for third-party service integrations
- Security-First Design
Sensitive value redaction, command injection prevention, cryptographic validation, and fail-closed architecture
- Rich Consent Experience
Modern UX for managing OAuth2 delegations with design system compliance
- Comprehensive Audit Logging
Structured JSON logging for compliance and security monitoring
Frameworks like FastMCP can implement the whole OAuth2.1 ceremonies as mandated by the MCP spec but this means that you have to configure it for every MCP Server you deploy and maintain it. You also have to configure secure storage and basically run a multitude of OAuth2 authorization servers. With the identity broker and a gateway you can dumb down MCP server development to only provide tools on the target technology you want. OAuth2 ceremonies, token vaulting and token translation are done transparently. Because token exchange is done centrally via a gateway, this allows agents to interact with hundreds of MCP servers via one channel.
If you want to offer an MCP server to your customers as part of your SaaS, the identity broker can provide an additional consent surface that records which agents were actually used. With centralized tool authorization, you can keep an audit trail of approvals on your side regardless of which agent the customer runs.
The agentic identity broker can simplify agents by requiring only a single user token that can be used with an arbitrary number of MCP servers. When paired with a portal for user interactions, token procurement can be front-loaded in the portal, and the agent's responsibility is to forward this token to upstream MCP servers via a gateway.
The impersonation feature allows to start delegation chains via privileged clients, like a Google Chat or Slack bridge. The broker can be instructed to trust for two independent machine identities to assume the session for a particular user. This allows to use the permissions of a user on the company chat in another third-party system.
The tool approval support in the broker allows to enforce tool calls independent of the agent interface in use. This allows a last resort check before emails get sent or documents shared with a central audit trail.
Check out the following docs:
- Quickstart — Get started with Agentic Identity Broker in minutes.
- agenticidentitybroker.dev – Underlying concepts, guides and API specs.
The architecture overview describes the system design, component boundaries, and domain glossary.
Agentic Identity Broker has a built-in consent management UI:
For contribution rules, test commands, and coverage reports, see CONTRIBUTING.md.
Agentic Identity Broker is currently in active development. We use this project in production internally for several MCP servers and have seen good potential. We are coding in the open to gauge our approach. If you find it useful, let us know. If you'd like a feature that's missing, open an issue in our GitHub repo.
While this project was created by professionals with decades of experience in the identity space (including building multiple OIDC and OAuth2 providers), it was developed with a strong focus on agentic engineering and spec-driven development. We review every PR and prioritize sound engineering practices over convenience.
Major roadmap topics include: (a) formalizing token exchange for agent-to-agent calls, (b) intent based authorization and (c) user facing acticity logs.
Thanks to all contributors who are helping to make the Agentic Identity Broker better.
Agentic Identity Broker is a Zalando Engineering project.

FAA Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:03:24 UTC
00:03:24 KST

Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control as Part of Ongoing Modernization Effort Deployment of Brand New Air Traffic Control Continues at Record Pace
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system.
The Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) replaces four systems dating back to the 1980s that are in more than 400 FAA facilities. E-IDS provides a single, secure system that gives air traffic controllers faster access to information they need. It also will reduce costly repairs and workarounds while enhancing safety for the American flying public.
The first five facilities to receive these upgrades include:
- Atlantic City International Airport
- Nashville International Airport
- Greater Rochester International Airport
- Data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City
The FAA plans to install E-IDS in 435 sites by the end of 2028.
“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system, and under President Trump, we’re delivering just that. The installation of E-IDS is just the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
Click HERE or above to watch a video on the new technology.
“E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System.”
You can track the progress of the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) by state and airport on our Modern Skies website.
Additional information:
E-IDS is a digital display board that puts important operational information in one place so controllers can quickly see updates, status information, and alerts they need to keep air traffic moving safely and efficiently. This information includes notices about equipment issues and disruptions, air traffic conditions, weather impacts, and important advisories.
E-IDS will also improve how Pilot Reports (PIREPS) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. PIREPs are first-hand reports on weather conditions from pilots to air traffic controllers. Both provide vital information on real-time pilot conditions and improve situational awareness for controllers.
Reminder:
Under Secretary Duffy’s leadership, the FAA is rapidly moving to make upgrades to our air traffic control system nationwide. We have already:
- Replaced 69% of copper wires
- Installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers
- Transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips
- Installed 226 IP Voice Switches

Where Each U.S. State Gets Its Tax Revenue From
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:02:07 UTC
00:02:07 KST

How the 50 States Generate Their Tax Revenue
Key Takeaways
- Property taxes are the largest individual tax category in 25 states, including Florida, Texas, and New York.
- Washington collects nearly half of its combined state and local tax revenue from general sales and gross receipts taxes.
- Delaware stands out for license taxes, reflecting its role as a legal home for businesses.
From paychecks and purchases to homes and businesses, states rely on different combinations of taxes to fund public services.
This graphic breaks down combined state and local tax revenue across all 50 states using 2024 government finance data from the U.S. Census Bureau. The percentages show each category’s share of tax collections, excluding federal taxes and funding such as federal grants.
Property Taxes Lead in Half the Country
Property taxes are the largest revenue source in half of U.S. states, with particularly high shares in New Hampshire (64.3%), Alaska (42.4%), and Texas (41.1%). General sales and gross receipts taxes lead in 16 states, while individual income taxes top the list in seven.
The country’s largest states illustrate these differences. Individual income taxes dominate in California, while property taxes narrowly exceed general sales taxes in Florida and individual income taxes in New York.
Including local governments makes a substantial difference. In Texas, for example, property taxes are collected by local tax authorities and support services such as schools, roads, and fire protection, even though the state government itself levies no property tax.
These shares describe how governments raise money, rather than how much an individual household owes. A large property-tax share can reflect limited collections from other taxes as well as substantial property-tax revenue.
How States Fund Services Without Taxing Wages
Florida collects no individual income tax revenue, with property and general sales taxes together supplying about three-quarters of state and local tax collections. In Texas, those two categories account for nearly 79%, highlighting both states’ reliance on property and consumption taxes.
New Hampshire takes that pattern further: property taxes generated 64.3% of tax revenue, the highest share nationwide. The state has no general sales tax and does not tax wages. Its small individual income tax share in 2024 reflects the interest and dividends tax, which was repealed effective in 2025.
Sales-related collections also extend beyond the checkout counter. General sales taxes include taxes on business gross receipts, while selective sales taxes apply to particular products or activities, such as fuel, tobacco, and utilities. This helps explain why a state’s revenue mix can look different from the taxes shoppers encounter directly.
Delaware and North Dakota: The Outliers
Delaware’s largest revenue source is license taxes, accounting for roughly one-third of collections. This category includes corporate franchise licenses and related charges, giving it a much broader meaning than driver’s licenses or hunting permits.
That revenue source connects to Delaware’s position in corporate America. In 2024, the state was the legal home of more than two million business entities and about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies. Incorporation generates public revenue from businesses whose operations extend far beyond Delaware’s borders.
North Dakota’s unusual mix reflects another economic advantage: natural resources. “Other taxes,” which include severance taxes on resource extraction, supplied 40.7% of collections. The state levies taxes on oil and gas production and oil extraction, linking part of its public finances to the value of energy produced within its borders.
Learn More on the Voronoi App
To explore the role of property taxes worldwide, check out Revenues from property taxes are much higher in advanced economies on Voronoi.

RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
15:01:38 UTC
00:01:38 KST

Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”
Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.
Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.
EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.
The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.
In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”
There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.
In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”
Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.
Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”
At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.
Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.
However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.
Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.
Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

====================================================================================================

In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.
In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”
There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.
In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”
Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.
Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”
At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.
Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.
However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.
Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.
Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

Lippitt-Knoster in Practice (Field Notes for Managing Complex Projects)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
14:57:16 UTC
23:57:16 KST

"Lippitt-Knoster" is one of those things where if you've worked with me during the last 10 years, you've likely heard me mention it. You might even be reading this because I needed somewhere to point you. In which case, Hi! 👋
The Lippitt-Knoster Model for Managing Complex Change was originally written to describe a way of navigating large organizational shifts, but I’ve found that it’s also useful as a diagnosis tool for any kind of large and long-running project. After all, every project is a "change" in a microcosm. You might not have a complex organizational change to manage every day, but everyone is involved in long-running projects of some size and shape in a company. So that’s what I use it for, and it is useful indeed.
The beauty of the model is that you don’t need an MBA or a special issue of the Harvard Business Review to explain it. It says that any complex project requires six components to succeed, and if one or another is missing, you’ll have some specific and corresponding failure.
It can be summed up in a simple chart but also rewards you with some deeper insights as you apply it:
- Vision is the purpose and endpoint of a project. Vision tells you where you’re going and why. If the vision is missing, there will be confusion about what is being done and why work is happening.
- Consensus is a team's agreement and alignment around the vision. If a team lacks consensus, people will not want to do the thing and they will sabotage you.
- Incentives are the motivation or reasons for why people support the work and prioritize it appropriately. If not everyone is incentivized properly, there will be resistance. Resistance is the passive sibling of sabotage.
- The Action Plan is the practical set of steps to get from vision to finish. If you lack an action plan, your team will experience a routine set of false starts and treadmills, which is another way of saying that it will look like work is happening but nothing actually moves forward. You won’t make progress.
- Resources are the organizational capacity (people, budget, time) needed to accomplish the work. Lacking resources is a close cousin to lacking skills; it leads to frustration in trying to do something you know you're capable of, but with an unrealistic set of operating constraints.
- Skills are the ability to do the work necessary to complete the project. If a team lacks the necessary skills, you'll have a lot of questions around if this work is possible, leading to anxiety.
Vision, consensus, and incentives are all Strategic Concerns. They involve abstract political work: ideas, relationships, people, and an understanding of the business. The action plan, skills, and resources are all Tactical Concerns. They are focused on the practical details of “how” something gets done.1
One mistake I often see people make is to focus primarily on one concern or the other. For example, a product manager or corporate strategist might spend too much time focused on the strategic side of things without understanding if the team or company is able to execute. Consequently, their ability to build consensus will be negatively impacted by not knowing what is possible or probable. Line managers and software engineers typically make the opposite mistake. They focus too much on the ‘how’ instead of the ‘why’. They’ll prove that something is possible and how it can be done, without realizing that sometimes the team or business doesn't want to do the thing they’re proposing. Neither myopia ends in a successful project.
The order of the model components matters – they flow into each other – but can be managed in either direction. For example: you might start with a vision, build consensus, arrange the right incentives for everyone to act, create a plan, provide adequate resources and timeline to accomplish that plan, and make sure it is staffed with people who have the skills to execute on it. Easy peasy!
You could also navigate the components the other way, working through a series of questions: is something possible? Do skills exist to accomplish the thing? Do those skills (people) have excess capacity that can be allocated to this idea? Can it be done without budget? Can that group of people be small enough that they organically develop their own plans? And if so, are they incentivized to take on this kind of work outside their daily responsibilities? Does it need sign-off from anyone? If you’ve found confirmatory answers along the way, congratulations: you can carve out a secret R&D initiative within your team or your company. (This is also 'effectuation' in practice.)
You can also read the model from the perspectives of both cause and effect. Reading it one way creates a checklist before kicking off any major work: “Here are the six prerequisites for success, are we all set?” (A causal, prescriptive reading – given starting parameters, what will be the end result?) Reading it backwards turns it into a troubleshooting tool. For example, if someone comes to you mid-project complaining that "We keep going in circles and the team is anxious! What can I do?" you might look at the model and respond, "Well of course! You don't have an action plan. Or maybe, it hasn't been adequately distributed and communicated and people feel that they lack the skills to accomplish something so big. Let's break it down into manageable pieces that we do have the skills for." It’s pretty quick to go between looking at the failure states and looking at the necessary components to diagnose what’s going on with a project. (A diagnostic reading, reasoning backwards.)
The model is a fantastic tool for making sense of things. But that leaves the hard work to start after you've made sense of things. How do you drive consensus? How do you align folks around a vision? How do you build up skills, or break down big projects into smaller pieces for which skills exist? How do you win resources, or align incentives?
Some of those answers are obvious, but most are not. Many of the answers are best understood as the manifestation of tacit expertise — a ‘feeling’ for the right move in any particular context, a form of expertise that comes from having been around the block a few times.
And like with most tacit expertise, you’ll find that there are no one-size-fits-all answers to any scenario, but there are plenty of good practices and useful observations.
So here are some of mine:
Strategic Concerns
The most common and important questions that come up after someone lays out a vision are “Why should we do this?” and permutations around the follow-up details. If you see those questions, that’s “confusion”, which is another way of saying you’ve presented a fantasy instead of a vision (or perhaps, the vision is missing entirely). That’s because many people confuse vision for having a colorful and inspiring imagination, making their picture too colorful, unrealistically grand, or too far off.2
My experience is that you make more progress by simply providing adequate context and letting people derive their own vision. The art of context is giving people breadcrumbs to get from where you are today to where you want to be in the future, and giving them some good reasons to follow those breadcrumbs with you. There’s nothing more effective than a self-motivated team that thinks they’re the ones who came up with the idea, that they saw what things could be like. That’s vision.
Similarly, consensus is a straightforward concept, but strangely elusive in most organizations. Any organization beyond a certain age and size will typically have a 'minimally viable consensus' while practically being at odds with itself. Departments often turn into silos with their own internal logic for what should happen. Job security encourages teams to think about what’s best for them instead of for the company. And companies don’t do a great job tying “what’s best for the company” with “what’s best for the individuals within, or the communities around”,3 which makes most employment mercenary: people naturally find a balance between what they’re paid and how much to care about the thing in question. (In that sense, incorporated businesses are kind of like democracy: a bad choice, but among the best of the options available for coordinating large groups of people to accomplish things.)
Recognizing that, one amateur mistake people make is trying to build consensus in a group setting. It just doesn't happen that way. You’re either going to have everyone nodding along and afraid to say their piece in front of everyone else, or you’re going to have one guy (and it’s usually a guy – sorry, my dudes) start pulling some “what about”-ism and dragging the conversation into a black hole of details that you never intended to argue about but find yourself frustratingly debating anyway.
In either scenario, the meeting will end without consensus.
In Japanese business culture there is a concept called “nemawashi”, which translates roughly to “tending to the roots” or “laying the groundwork”. It’s a good analogy because the practice of creating consensus requires a lot of political skill, footwork, trust-building, and private conversation. It means giving people space to tell you everything that’s wrong with your idea, finding ways to address those concerns, and making sure everyone is aligned before the alignment actually happens. The group meeting when everyone signs off in agreement should be the result of careful stage management — you should know and have already addressed everyone’s concerns, including second-order effects of how addressing one person’s issues will impact others.
There should be no surprises; it is theater, not improv.
That said, you might not be able to get to consensus. Perhaps your boss wants the “thing” to happen but there’s another department that’s actively against it. Maybe you're encroaching on their turf, or it will reduce their capacity in some zero-sum resource bucket. Maybe they just have a different perspective on the world and the approaches the business should take. Maybe you've wandered into a long-running feud and this project is just one of many different battles being waged. Who knows, people can be both petty and complicated!
If you can't get their buy-in, they will sabotage it in all sorts of creative ways. Because sabotage and resistance are close cousins and are political (in the sense of not being open conflict), monographs on activism and subterfuge can be read as useful primers. Consider James C. Scott's Weapons of the Weak and the OSS's Simple Sabotage Field Manual for what kinds of foot dragging, malicious compliance, noncompliance, evasion, sowing confusion, slander, useless meetings, arbitrary hurdles, revisiting decisions, and moving goalposts to expect.
My advice for these scenarios is to try one of two things. Your first option is to get to the bottom of why there is no consensus and figure out if you’re in a position to address that root cause. Often, you’re not in a position to address those things; if you pursue resolution, you’re going to use up a lot of your political capital or burn out trying to get the project moving forward. And success can be fleeting – projects can continue to be sabotaged even after launch. I once had a project launch only to have all of its resources immediately pulled, forcing its premature death.
Not even chief executives are immune to this; sometimes the solution to a lack of consensus and active sabotage is to simply fire the people in disagreement. (Obviously, use this technique sparingly — you’re scorching the earth.)
So I recommend most people take the second approach, which is to just drop it. Move on. It’s a lost cause. Don’t be the sailor with a bucket trying to dump water off this Titanic. Quitting things and dropping things is a totally acceptable thing to do; life isn’t a video game where you’re striving for 100% completeness on every side quest. Move on to things where you’re actually making a difference.
But let’s say everyone agrees. Now you need to make sure that things are prioritized appropriately. You’re not going to make any progress if this is low on everyone’s priority list. So you incentivize teams and people.
Positive incentives typically work better than negative incentives, but most people are not in a position to offer meaningful (financial) incentives to push a project forward. Instead, you can rely on horse-trading (“if you help me move this project forward, I’ll help with your thing”), you can help people resolve their problems, and you can paint a compelling-enough end-state that people also want to reach that goal with you.
Otherwise, people are going to be resistant, which is a passive form of sabotage: sabotage without commitment, or general apathy. It might not even be malicious. It’s just… well, you’re just one more project for people to care about and work on. Why should they do it above all else?
And more importantly, resistance can turn into sabotage when incentives are not just missing, but misaligned. Misaligned incentives can break consensus when you're sweating the details.
Tactical Concerns
Now, let’s say you figured out the strategic bits and you’re working through the implementation portion. Some projects are simple enough that you can just describe what needs to be done, and you can count those requirements on a single maimed hand. We’re not talking about those projects.
Any complex-enough project requires coordination of requirements, dependencies, timelines, people, and other details. I’ve written a bit about those issues in “When Everything is Important But Nothing Is Getting Done”, so I don’t want to retread too much ground.
But one thing worth highlighting is how skills and anxiety are coupled, and how to navigate a lack of skills. Any ambitious project is at some point going to run into a lack of skills or prior experience because the work wouldn't be ambitious if you'd done it before. So in many regards, it is an existential question for any project: are you and your team able to do what needs to be done? If not, you’ll get a very stressed team, or you’ll get a simulacrum of what you expected.
There are ways to compensate for a lack of skills. I rely on three techniques:
First is up-skilling people. Education, mentorship, and training are effective ways to turn juniors into seniors, low-skilled employees into high-skilled employees. While there are a variety of documented techniques for this (see: accelerated expertise, tactical decision games), the caveats are that (a) this typically takes longer than the time-span of a single project and (b) you need to find people who are interested in learning.
So the second technique is atomization: break the requirements into smaller pieces that meet the level of skill available rather than trying to get people to rise to the required level. Instead of making everyone work harder, just make the requirements easier. Instead of asking people to “cut database reads by 50%” or “create a capacity forecasting model for the next 12 months” (where they may not even know where to start), give them smaller tasks and directions for what to do to accomplish that. Point folks in the right direction, explain the what and the why, turn big asks into a series of steps, a recipe to accomplish something. This is in itself a form of teaching, and it is more project-sized (see what I did there?).
The third technique is to roll up your sleeves and contribute. I’ve learned from many effective leaders that there is no work below your pay grade. What makes many great leaders "great" is their willingness to spend extra time doing “glue” work, filling in the holes between roles, and making sure all assumptions are bridged back to real expectations. They are never too good to personally write up a project document, to manage a tracker, to make sure that people are talking to each other. They often know as much or more about the details than subject matter experts, but they don't needlessly meddle – they support where needed and use gaps as up-skilling opportunities.
Much of the work of compensating for skills gaps is directly translatable into managing budget, time, and effort tradeoffs to navigate the “resources” component of Lippitt-Knoster. And your ability to solve for skills and resources directly translates back into the specific action plan you need to put together. For example: you may decide not to spend $100,000 on a vendor because you can reverse engineer a single feature you need for a project, but you need to add time to the plan for that.
These considerations become a calculus of risks, rewards, and effort, which in turn underpins the strategic portions that we talked about earlier: sure, you might think you can lead a team to rebuild the hot new vendor in house in two months, but have you earned organizational political capital to place those chips on the table?
So there you have it, Lippitt-Knoster in practice. Lead on!
1 - This grouping is not present in most Lippitt-Knoster model descriptions I’ve come across; it is my own humble contribution. The order I'm presenting it in is also my contribution – the order in Mary Lippit's original 1987 model is quite different, for reasons I couldn't discern.
2 - A realistic vision that is too far into the future is its own type of risk – every day presents new opportunities for conditions to change, starting conditions to be led astray. The likelihood of any far-off future has too many compounding variables... too many things have to go right and be true for it to be reliable enough to pin your hopes to.
3 - These things are usually at odds with each other. There's a big literature about how "equity" is a tool to get employees to care about corporate success, but most startup equity goes to zero; for the average employee, a bonus or a pay raise is more useful. Public company equity presents a different issue: it is dependent on public market behavior, and less on your individual ability to impact it – being in a public company, you're likely one of thousands-plus of employees.

MTG-I2 First Images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
14:35:29 UTC
23:35:29 KST

Europe’s meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite’s launch on 27 August 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings.
Captured from geostationary orbit, some 36,000 km above the Earth, the image acquired on 20 October captures Europe, Africa and the Atlantic in remarkable detail, revealing intricate cloud formations stretching across the North Atlantic, contrasting with the largely clear skies over the Sahara.
While the full-disc image captures a single moment in time, an accompanying rapid-scan animation brings Europe’s weather to life, showing how cloud formations and weather systems evolve through observations taken just 2.5 minutes apart. This offers a glimpse of MTG-I2’s future operational service, which will enable meteorologists to monitor rapidly changing weather conditions over Europe more closely.
These first data follow the handover of MTG-I2 to EUMETSAT’s Mission Control Centre on 9 September, after the successful completion of the Launch and Early Orbit Phase. The satellite is still undergoing calibration and validation, working with the European Space Agency and European industry, to prepare it for operational service, which is expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027.
“This first image, and the animation, is a milestone for EUMETSAT and for our Member States,” EUMETSAT Director-General Phil Evans said. “Just two months after launch, MTG-I2 shows us what rapid scanning will make possible: a much timelier view of fast-developing weather over Europe. As extreme events become more frequent and intense, forecasters and emergency services will be able to see hazards evolve more precisely and act sooner.”
MTG-I2 will empower EUMETSAT’s Member States with a rapid scan service that will deliver high-resolution observations of the European continent every 2.5 minutes. By capturing changes in cloud formations at such rapid intervals, MTG-I2 will help forecasters follow the development of severe weather much more closely. This is especially valuable for fast-developing storms, which can bring heavy rainfall, hail, strong winds and flash floods. Timelier observations will also support earlier, more precise warnings and help emergency response during extreme events, including wildfires.
MTG-I2 is operated by EUMETSAT from its headquarters in Darmstadt, Germany. The satellite was developed by the European Space Agency with Thales Alenia Space as industry prime contractor, fulfilling the requirements set by EUMETSAT in consultation with the meteorological services of its Member States.
Download the high-resolution first full-disc image from MTG-I2 here.

Black Beans and Rice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

If you’ve got the main dish sorted but no idea what to serve with it, this easy Black Beans and Rice is the one to bookmark! I’m always amazed at how much flavor you can get from a few simple and affordable ingredients. Tender rice, soft black beans, sweet bell pepper, and plenty of garlic and cumin make this SO much more exciting than a scoop of plain rice. Everything comes together in one pan with canned beans (so no soaking), and at just $0.94 per serving, it’s a tasty addition to dinner that won’t put a dent in your grocery budget!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Little More Exciting Than Plain Rice
Our Louisiana style red beans and rice is a classic, but starting with dried beans means soaking and a much longer cooking time. This black beans and rice takes a much easier route! I sauté the onion and bell pepper with cumin and cayenne to build a savory, yet slightly sweet base, then add the garlic, rice and vegetable broth. Once the rice is tender, I gently stir in the canned black beans and let everything warm through. There’s no separate pot of rice, no lengthy simmer, and lots of delicious flavor. 😋
If you’ve ever made our quick seasoned black beans, you’ll recognize that delicious garlic-and-cumin combination here, too. The difference is that this recipe works those flavors into the rice, with the beans added at the end. But what I love most about this recipe (besides how cheap it is!) is how nutritious and filling it ends up being. Black beans add plant-based protein and fiber, rice brings comforting carbs, and the veggies add plenty of flavor and texture. Finish with fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lime if you’ve got some, and you’ve got a satisfying side dish that’s also handy for meal prep.
Recipe Success Tips
- Stick with long-grain white rice. I use Walmart brand long-grain white rice for this recipe, which takes about 15 minutes to simmer, followed by a 5-10 minute covered rest. Not all rice cooks the same, though! Different brands and varieties can absorb liquid at different rates, so always check that your rice is tender before adding the beans. I wouldn’t swap in brown rice or instant rice without adjusting the liquid and cooking time, as they cook quite differently (follow the package directions for this).
- Keep the rice at a gentle simmer. Once the broth comes to a boil, turn the heat down to low and let it cook. You only want a gentle simmer here, not lots of vigorous bubbling. Too much heat can make the broth evaporate before the rice finishes cooking, leaving you with hard grains or rice stuck to the bottom of the pan.
- Save the black beans for last. One of my favorite things about using canned black beans is that they’re already cooked, so there’s no extra work involved! Just drain and rinse them to remove the salty canning liquid, then gently fold them into the tender rice with the cilantro. Adding them at the end means they only need warming through. This stops them from getting too soft or breaking apart as the rice cooks.
What to Serve with Black Beans and Rice
This black beans and rice recipe makes four 1-cup servings, which I’d say is plenty for a generous side dish. BUT it’s also really easy to turn into a filling dinner with a few extras! I always make a batch of shredded chicken at the start of each week for my family and keep it in the fridge for easy meals, so I’ll sometimes mix some into the rice with fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lime. That turns a simple side dish into a more substantial meal with hardly any extra cooking! For a meat-free option that’s also perfect for meal prep, I love adding my baked tofu with a drizzle of lime crema.
Planning a Mexican-inspired night at home? I’d serve these rice and beans alongside our saucy cheese enchiladas with a generous spoonful of fresh pico de gallo for some crunch, too! I’d get the enchiladas started first, then prepare the rice so everything is ready around the same time. So good, and much cheaper than ordering takeout!
how to make Black Beans and Rice Step-By-Step Photos
Gather all of your ingredients: Drain and rinse one 15.25 oz. can of black beans to remove the canning liquid, then set aside.
Prep the fresh ingredients: Finely dice ½ a yellow onion (about ½ cup) and 1 green bell pepper (about ¾ cup). Mince 2 cloves of garlic (about 1 tsp) and 2 Tbsp of fresh cilantro.
Sauté the vegetables and spices: Add the diced ½ onion, diced 1 bell pepper, 1 Tbsp olive oil, ½ tsp salt, ½ tsp black pepper, 2 tsp cumin, and ⅛ tsp cayenne to a sauté pan over medium heat. Stir everything together and cook for about 5 minutes, or until the onions look glossy and the bell pepper starts to soften. The vegetables should be gently sizzling, and the spices should smell fragrant.
Add the garlic: Stir in the 2 cloves of minced garlic and cook for another 2 minutes, stirring occasionally. The garlic should become fragrant without turning dark brown. If it starts browning too quickly, lower the heat slightly so it doesn’t burn.
Stir in the rice and broth: Add 1 cup of uncooked long-grain white rice and 2½ cups of vegetable broth to the pan. Stir everything together so the rice and vegetables are evenly distributed throughout the broth.
Cover and simmer: Add 1 Tbsp butter, cover the pan with a lid, and bring the mixture to a boil. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low and let it simmer for about 15 minutes, or until the rice has absorbed most of the liquid. The rice should be tender, with very little liquid remaining in the pan. If your rice needs a longer cooking time, follow the guidance on the package. You can add a little extra broth if the rice is still too firm, but keep in mind this may give it a softer, more risotto-like texture.
Add the black beans and cilantro: Fluff the cooked rice gently with a fork, then stir in the drained and rinsed black beans and 2 Tbsp minced cilantro. Replace the lid, remove the pan from the heat, and let everything sit, covered, for 5-10 minutes. The residual heat will help warm the beans through while the rice finishes resting.
Fluff and serve: Give the black beans and rice one final gentle fluff with a fork, making sure the beans are warmed through, then serve hot. Enjoy!
sTORAGE & rEHEATING
This black beans and rice is handy for meal prep! I recommend dividing leftovers into individual, shallow airtight containers so they cool quickly and are ready for easy lunches or dinners throughout the week. Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking and store for up to 3-4 days.
Reheating
Rice tends to dry out a little in the fridge, but that’s an easy fix. Add a splash of water or vegetable broth to your portion, cover, and microwave until heated through, stirring halfway to avoid cold spots. You can also reheat it in a covered saucepan over medium-low heat, adding a little liquid to help soften the rice.
Whichever method you use, make sure the rice and beans reach 165°F throughout before serving. I recommend reheating only what you plan to eat.
Freezing
For longer storage, portion the black beans and rice into freezer-safe containers or bags and freeze for up to 3 months. Smaller portions are easier to thaw and reheat, and they’re handy when you only need a quick side dish! Thaw overnight in the refrigerator, then reheat using either method above. The rice may be slightly softer after freezing, but a splash of broth can help if it seems dry.
Got More Black Beans in the Pantry? Try These Recipes Next
- Our Smoky Black Bean Soup is thick, hearty, and full of rich, smoky flavor from fire-roasted tomatoes and smoked paprika. Ready in just 25 minutes, it’s another delicious way to turn canned beans into a satisfying meal.
- These Hearty Black Bean Quesadillas are loaded with black beans, sweet corn, cilantro, and melty cheddar cheese. They’re crispy on the outside, cheesy in the middle, and freezer-friendly, too.
- My creamy Black Bean Dip is packed with sautéed jalapeños, garlic, and tangy lime, then topped with melted cheddar cheese, so grab some tortilla chips and dig in!
Check out our collection of black bean recipes for even more budget-friendly meal ideas!

After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct.
The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.
The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.
The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa, and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.
The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.
The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist. The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks.
As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September, further.

TikTok&#8217;s For You page needs to change, says the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
14:00:49 UTC
23:00:49 KST

The European Commission claims TikTok broke its online platform rules by offering a recommendation algorithm that creates a “rabbit hole effect” on users. In an announcement on Friday, the regulators allege TikTok’s algorithm can harm users with “endless and repeated exposure” to content related to sadness, isolation, or body image.
TikTok’s For You page needs to change, says the EU
The EU Commission says TikTok’s ‘rabbit hole’ effect can pose harm to users.
The findings come months after the EU Commission declared that TikTok’s design is too “addictive.” While TikTok has implemented controls to mitigate the algorithm’s “rabbit hole effect,” the Commission says its preliminary findings suggest that they’re not effective. TikTok must now change the design of its For You feed, or else face fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover. The platform is also facing pressure in the US, with lawmakers and a wave of lawsuits raising concerns about child safety.
Since enacting the Digital Services Act in 2023 — a set of rules that hold tech companies legally accountable for their impact on users— the EU Commission has targeted several companies for allegedly violating the regulations, including X, Meta, Temu, and AliExpress. As reported by Politico, this is the first time the Commission has cited a recommendation algorithm as the reason for a breach.
“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” Henna Virkkunen, the EU Commission’s executive vice president of tech sovereignty, security, and democracy, says in the press release. “Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”

Amazon is adding a new feature to Alexa for Shopping that allows customers to purchase items by texting the AI shopping assistant. Users can describe the products they’re looking to buy and/or provide a photograph of the item, and Alexa for Shopping will search for matching results in Amazon listings, text back with recommendations, and order the item on the users’ behalf.
Amazon will let you text Alexa your shopping list
The Alexa for Shopping AI assistant can now order groceries and recommend products over text messages.
This launch builds on the existing Alexa for Shopping experience that launched in May, allowing users to place orders during moments where texting is more convenient than using Amazon’s app or website. The contact will appear in your phone as “Amazon Alexa,” and can be used for a wide range of shopping requests, including ordering weekly groceries, asking for gift recommendations, finding similar products to something you’ve snapped a photo of, and more. Alexa says it remembers your personal preferences over time (so if you frequently ask for vegan options, it’ll bear that in mind for product recommendations), and can track deals and prices to text you when an item you’re watching has gone on sale.
The texting capability is rolling out to a small group of Amazon customers in the US starting today, who will receive a text message inviting them to try the experience. It will then roll out to “millions more customers” in the coming weeks, according to Amazon’s announcement.
“Customers often jot down what they need the moment they think of it in their notes, in their messages, in their group chats,” said Rajiv Mehta, vice president of Conversational Shopping at Amazon. “Now with Alexa for Shopping, your personal shopping agent is just a text away. Message it what you need and Alexa goes to work on your behalf — searching, comparing, and buying so you can get on with your day.”
Amazon is one of several companies that have introduced ways to text their chatbots. Last month saw OpenAI launching a feature that allows users to exchange text messages with its personal AI agent, Dot. DoorDash also introduced a text-based ordering feature in September that lets users get dish recommendations and order food by texting the Ask DoorDash AI chatbot.

How to Get Signed &#038; Personalized Books From Me For the Holidays, 2026 Edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
13:44:26 UTC
22:44:26 KST

How to Get Signed & Personalized Books From Me For the Holidays, 2026 Edition
Posted on November 6, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 2 Comments
We’ve come to that time of the year again, where folks begin to think about their holiday gift giving, and at least some of you think about books as the perfect gift. Well, they are! But would make them even more perfect is getting those books signed and personalized. Every year I join forces with Jay and Mary’s Book Center in Troy, Ohio, to sign and personalize books so that you’ll have them available to give to the people you love, including yourself.
From today (Nov. 6) through Friday, December 4, you can order books I have written from Jay and Mary’s and I will come in and sign them for you, and then the bookstore will ship them to you (US only). I strongly encourage you to get your orders in early, so there are no delays in shipping the books to you this holiday season.
Here’s how to do it!
1. Call Jay & Mary’s at their number (937 335 1167) and let them know that you’d like to order signed copies of my books. Please call rather than send e-mail; they find it easier to keep track of things that way.
2. Tell them which books you would like (For example, Monsters of Ohio ), and what, if any, names you would like the book signed to. If there’s something specific you’d like written in the books let them know, but for their sake and mine, please keep it short. Also, if you’re ordering the book as a gift, make sure you’re clear about whose name the book is being signed to. If this is unclear, I will avoid using a specific name.
3. Order any other books you might think you’d like, written by other people, because hey, you’ve already called a bookstore for books, and helping local independent bookstores is a good thing. I won’t sign these, unless for some perverse reason you want me to, in which case, sure, why not.
4. Give them your mailing address and billing information, etc.
5. And that’s it! Shortly thereafter I will go to the store and sign your books for you.
Again, the deadline for signed/personalized books for 2026 is December 4. After December 4 all Scalzi stock will still be signed and available, but I will likely not be able to personalize.
Also, this is open to US addresses only. Sorry, rest of the world. It’s a cost of shipping thing.
What books are available?
CURRENT HARDCOVER: The current hardcover is Monsters of Ohio. There might be hardcovers of When the Moon Hits Your Eye and The Shattering Peace, both of which came out last year, but you should inquire because stock on those would be limited.
CURRENT TRADE PAPERBACK: As of now, all seven books the Hugo-winning Old Man’s War series (Old Man’s War, The Ghost Bridages, The Last Colony, Zoe’s Tale, The Human Division, The End of All Things, The Shattering Piece) are available in trade paperback with matching cover treatments, so if you wanted to give those seven books as a gift, they are all now a matching set. Other books in trade paperback: When the Moon Hits Your Eye, Starter Villain, The Kaiju Preservation Society, The Android’s Dream, Agent to the Stars and Fuzzy Nation, Redshirts (the 2013 Hugo Award winner), Twenty-First Century Science Fiction (which features a story of mine), Metatropolis (which I edited and contribute a novella to) are all also available in trade paperback format. Also available: Robots Vs. Fairies, the anthology that features the story of mine that was adapted for the “Three Robots” episode of the Netflix animated series Love, Death and Robots.
CURRENT MASS MARKET PAPERBACK: The Mass Market Paperback format is being phased out and stocks of it will become increasingly scarce over time (and the series I have in the format will migrate to trade paperback format eventually). That said, at the moment both my Interdependency series (The Collapsing Empire, The Consuming Fire, The Last Emperox) and my Lock In series (Lock In, Head On, companion novella Unlocked) are still available for purchase.
CURRENT NON-FICTION: Your Hate Mail Will Be Graded (essay collection, Hugo winner).
AUDIOBOOKS: The Kaiju Preservation Society, The Last Emperox, The Consuming Fire, The Collapsing Empire, The Dispatcher, The End of All Things, Lock In, Head On, The Human Division, Redshirts, Fuzzy Nation, The God Engines, Metatropolis and Agent to the Stars are all available on CD and/or MP3 CD, and Jay & Mary’s should be able to special order them for you. Check with them about other titles, which may or may not be currently available on CD.
Two things regarding audiobooks: First, if you want these, you should probably call to order these as soon as possible. Second, and this is important, because the audiobooks come shrinkwrapped, I will have to remove the shrinkwrap in order to sign the cover. You ordering a signed audiobook means you’re okay with me doing that and with Jay & Mary’s shipping it to you out of its shrinkwrap.
If you have any other questions, drop them in the comment thread and I’ll try to answer them!

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation
You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.
Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.
More natural speech
You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.
Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.
More controllable, cinematic look
You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.
Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.
Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.
Real-world results, from creatives to global brands
Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.
Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
- For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
- For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.
- For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
13:02:16 UTC
22:02:16 KST

AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.
One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.
The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.
You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.
You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.
All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.
While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.
This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.
Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.
“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.
In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.
