Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.
His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.
Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.
“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Vigan says.
Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.
Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.
Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.
In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.
SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.
However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high-fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of lidar capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.
“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

OpenAI Finds 948 Local Privilege Escalation Bugs in the Linux Kernel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
12:59:43 UTC
21:59:43 KST

OpenAI Finds 948 Local Privilege Escalation Bugs In The Linux Kernel
OpenAI published a blog post outlining their work on autonomous vulnerability discovery. To showcase their AI potential, they found 948 valid local privilege escalation vulnerabilities within the Linux kernel.
OpenAI's prototype found 2,308 candidate vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and ultimately found 948 local privilege escalation exploits for allowing unprivileged local users to gain root access. They also generated candidate patches for maintainer review.
Discovering nearly one thousand local privilege escalation vulnerabilities consumed $1.2 million USD in API credits.
OpenAI researchers noted in their blog post:
"Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities."
Another interesting takeaway is that their GPT-5.5 Cyber model is finding more than 5x more novel LPEs than their GPT-5.6 Sol model despite three months of hardening/patches in the Linux kernel between scans.
Those wanting to go through this OpenAI showcase in more detail can do so via their blog post.

Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
11:57:16 UTC
20:57:16 KST

Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam.
Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam
Europe is witnessing a wave of protests against data centers.
Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.”
Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data centers until 2030, after a temporary stop that was announced at the end of 2023. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place. The site, being built by British developer Pure Data Centres, has also managed to navigate some loopholes to reach the construction stage.
The protests over Microsoft’s data center site in Amsterdam comes in the same week that activists staged a mock Israeli military checkpoint outside a Microsoft data center in Dublin on Tuesday, part of a wave of data center protests across Europe. Earlier this week, voters across the US also rejected unrestrained development of data centers. AI data centers are continuing to pop up across the US, with frequent opposition from locals concerned about the impact on their communities.
Microsoft also abandoned the UK’s largest data center project last month, after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s. The software maker has also faced a wave of protests from former employees over the past year. Microsoft’s 50th anniversary party was interrupted by employees protesting the use of Microsoft’s technologies in Israel’s war against Hamas, with one calling Microsoft’s AI CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, a “war profiteer.“
A Microsoft employee also disrupted the company’s Build developer conference last year, interrupting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s keynote. Months later, Microsoft fired two employee protesters who occupied its president’s office.

Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
11:50:10 UTC
20:50:10 KST

Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, according to CEO Elon Musk, who said on X that the company will use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercab robotaxis.
The decision to wind down the futuristic, steel-clad EV comes after just a few short years of underwhelming sales. When Musk handed over the first few Cybertrucks in late 2023, he predicted Tesla would sell around 250,000 per year. It was supposed to be such a cornerstone of Tesla’s future that, before construction began, the company talked about its Texas factory as the “Cybertruck factory.” But Tesla has instead sold just tens of thousands — total — over the last three years.
Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck at a moment when it is trying to become an AI- and robotics-focused company. A big part of that is its robotaxi ambitions.
The company has spent the last two months putting Cybercabs on the streets in its hometown of Austin, Texas. With no major incidents to date, the company has said it plans to expand the Cybercabs operations to other cities, starting with Dallas later this month. (Tesla also operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUVs in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, as well as three cities in Florida.)
This is the third product Tesla has discontinued in order to fuel those greater ambitions. Earlier this year, the company decided to end production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV and instead use the factory space dedicated to those vehicles to make Optimus humanoid robots.
First announced in 2019, the Cybertruck was a product that Musk had long obsessed over.
“Probably my personal favorite for the next product is the pickup truck, and we are going to just do an amazing pickup truck,” he said on one of Tesla’s earnings calls that year.
Musk promised the Cybertruck would be radical, inspired by the designs of cyberpunk sci-fi stories like “Blade Runner.” While that certainly bore out in the design, the company overpromised on the basics of the Cybertruck from the jump. During the now-infamous reveal event in 2019, when head designer Franz von Holzhausen cracked the Cybertruck’s windows with steel balls, Tesla said the EV was supposed to start at under $40,000 and have up to 500 miles of range. It achieved neither of those figures.
Instead, the truck was delayed for two years, in part because of the COVID-19 pandemic. When it finally did hit the market in late 2023, Tesla handed over the first few Cybertrucks to customers in a short, somewhat odd for Tesla event (by the company’s own standards, at least), which saw a poorly-lit Musk standing in a truck bed promising the truck was “the finest in apocalyptic equipment” fit for “late civilization vibes.” The base price had inflated to around $60,000, and the top-end range had shrunk by over 100 miles.
The truck has struggled on the market ever since. The polarizing design never seemed to sit well with buyers, especially at a higher-than-expected price. Then, during its first full year of sales in 2024, Musk became a major financial backer of Donald Trump, which turned the instantly recognizable Cybertruck into a target for protesters. That continued into 2025 as Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which fired thousands of federal workers.

We've built an open-source feature flag server for 11 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
11:40:06 UTC
20:40:06 KST

Unleash is a powerful open-source solution for feature management. It streamlines your development workflow, accelerates software delivery, and empowers teams to control how and when they roll out new features to end users. With Unleash, you can deploy code to production in smaller, more manageable releases at your own pace.
Feature flags in Unleash let you test your code with real production data, reducing the risk of negatively impacting your users' experience. It also enables your team to work on multiple features simultaneously without the need for separate feature branches.
Unleash is the most popular open-source solution for feature flagging on GitHub. It supports 15 official client and server SDKs and over 15 community SDKs. You can even create your own SDK if you wish. Unleash is compatible with any language and framework.
To get started with Unleash, you can either explore Unleash Enterprise with a free trial or get started locally with our open-source solution.
To start with Unleash Enterprise, request a free trial. This gives you access to a hosted instance with unlimited projects and environments and features such as role-based access control, change requests, single sign-on, and SCIM for automatic user provisioning.
To set up Unleash locally, you'll need git and docker installed on your machine.
Execute the following commands:
git clone git@github.com:Unleash/unleash.git
cd unleash
docker compose up -d
Then point your browser to localhost:4242 and log in using:
- username: admin
- password: unleash4all
If you'd rather run the source code in this repo directly via Node.js, see the step-by-step instructions to get up and running in the contributing guide.
Find your preferred SDK in our list of official SDKs and import it into your project. Follow the setup guides for your specific SDK.
If you use the docker compose file from the previous step, here's the configuration details you'll need to get going:
- For frontend SDKs, use:
  - URL: http://localhost:4242/api/frontend/
  - clientKey: default:development.unleash-insecure-frontend-api-token
- For backend SDKs, use:
  - Unleash API URL: http://localhost:4242/api/
  - API token: default:development.unleash-insecure-api-token
If you use a different setup, your configuration details will most likely also be different.
Checking the state of a feature flag in your code is easy! The syntax will vary depending on your language, but all you need is a simple function call to check whether a flag is available. Here's how it might look in Java:
if (unleash.isEnabled("AwesomeFeature")) {
  // do new, flashy thing
} else {
  // do old, boring stuff
}
Want to explore Unleash without setting it up locally? Here are two easy ways to see it in action.
Open a running Unleash environment in your browser with no signup or setup required. This shared demo instance includes the core functionality so you can quickly get a feel for how Unleash works.
Get your own dedicated instance with a free 14-day cloud trial. This includes the full Unleash Enterprise feature set; ideal when evaluating Unleash for production use.
To self-host Unleash in a production environment, you need to deploy it to a persistent server.
We provide guides for deploying to services like Heroku and DigitalOcean:
For more advanced configurations options, check out our documentation on:
We know that learning a new tool can be hard and time-consuming. We have a growing community that loves to help out. Please don't hesitate to reach out for help.
💬 Join Unleash on Slack if you want ask open questions about Unleash, feature toggling or discuss these topics in general.
💻 Create a GitHub issue if you have found a bug or have ideas on how to improve Unleash.
📚 Visit the documentation for more in-depth descriptions, how-to guides, and more.
📖 Learn more about the principles of building and scaling feature flag solutions.
Unleash is the largest open-source feature flag solution on GitHub. Building Unleash is a collaborative effort, and we owe a lot of gratitude to many smart and talented individuals. Building it together with the community ensures that we build a product that solves real problems for real people. We'd love to have your help too: Please feel free to open issues or provide pull requests.
Check out the CONTRIBUTING.md file for contribution guidelines and the Unleash developer guide for tips on environment setup, running the tests, and running Unleash from source. Before a pull request can be merged, contributors must read and agree to the Unleash Contributor License Agreement.
You can visit the Unleash documentation at https://docs.getunleash.io. As of 2 February 2026, the Unleash documentation source code lives in its own repository: Unleash/unleash-documentation.
- Get an overview of all feature flags across all your environments, applications and services
- Targeted releases using activation strategies to enable and disable features for certain users or segments without having to redeploy your application.
- Canary releases / gradual rollouts
- Kill switches
- A/B testing
- 2 environments
- Organize feature flags using tags
- Out-of-the-box integrations with popular tools (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Datadog) + integrate with anything with webhooks
- Insights for managing technical debt and stale flags
- API-first: everything can be automated. No exceptions.
- 12 official SDKs, and 10 community-contributed SDKs
- Run it via Docker with the official Docker image or as a pure Node.js application
- Privacy by design (GDPR and Schrems II). End-user data never leaves your application.
- Audit logs
- Enforce OWASP's secure headers via the strict HTTPS-only mode
- Flexible hosting options: host it on premise or in the cloud (any cloud)
- Scale with Unleash Edge independently of the Unleash server to support any number of frontend clients without overloading your Unleash instance
If you're looking for one of the following features, please take a look at our Pro and Enterprise plans:
- role-based access control (RBAC)
- single sign-on (SSO)
- more environments
- feature flags project support
- advanced segmentation
- additional strategy constraints
- tighter security
- more hosting options (we can even host it for you!)
Read more in the system overview section of the Unleash documentation.

Blue Origin Announces New Glenn Third Stage, New Booster Engine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Blue Origin Announces New Glenn Third Stage, New Booster Engine (space.com) 19
			
		 	
				Blue Origin has unveiled a third stage called GS3 for its New Glenn rocket, designed to deliver satellite constellations directly to geostationary orbit and support heavy-lift missions to the Moon and deep space. The company also announced Northstar, a new methalox booster engine that it says produces 715,000 pounds of thrust while cutting mass by 30% and parts by 50% compared with the BE-4. Space.com reports:  The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. (The other is SpaceX's Starship.) Blue Moon landing missions won't need to launch on GS3-equipped New Glenn rockets, according to Blue Origin. But the third stage "can support sustained operations around the moon," the company wrote in today's blog post. "By delivering significant payload mass directly to trans-lunar injection (TLI), GS3 enables faster transit times while preserving propellant for on-orbit operations." And there's already demand for such services: Blue Origin also announced today that a government customer (which it did not name) has booked a GS3 mission to cislunar (Earth-moon) space, with launch targeted for 2028.
And the company dropped yet more news today -- that it's working on a new first-stage engine, called Northstar. Like Blue Origin's other booster engine, the BE-4, Northstar burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant, a combination known as methalox. But the new engine is more powerful and less complex. "Compared to the BE-4 engine, Northstar reduces mass by 30% and parts count by 50%, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force," Blue Origin said in a second blog post today. "Manufacturing advancements have also significantly shortened production timelines, enabling assembly in less than a day." Northstar went from program approval to development testing in just 11 months, according to the company. But today's update did not say when the new engine will fly for the first time.

Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
10:42:52 UTC
19:42:52 KST

Tesla is getting the Cybertruck ready for retirement in an effort to ramp up its robotaxi output. In an X post on Friday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the company will be “winding down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory sometime around the middle of next year, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
Cybertruck production at the Texas Gigafactory is being axed to make way for more Cybercabs.
The production plant in Austin, Texas, is the only Tesla facility that’s known to assemble the Cybertruck, and that’s equipped to make the specialized components required to build the vehicles. Musk hasn’t mentioned if Cybertruck production will be moved elsewhere, but doing so would be arduous, especially for a car that’s never sold well. While Tesla doesn’t break out individual Cybertruck sales figures, even the highest analyst estimates place the total number of deliveries at roughly 70,000 since its launch in 2023 — significantly below the 250,000 that Musk once predicted would be sold annually.
The Cybertruck has also been mired in controversy since it was introduced, from its divisive design (that isn’t road legal in many parts of the world), the numerous recalls for faulty or outright dangerous components, and the fatal accidents it’s been involved in. It’s an unusually long and complicated history for a vehicle that’s only been on the road for three years. If the Cybertruck does meet its demise in 2027, Tesla still has another ridiculous vehicle on the horizon to serve as its spiritual successor.
